utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. As far as I can see, the appearances for both the Prosecution and the Defence are the same as they were yesterday. Thank you. Then I think we will continue now with the examination of the Prosecution witness, Mr. Kupusovic. Mr. Usher, could you please bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Could I just ask both general Galic and Mr. Kupusovic whether they hear me in a language they understand. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kupusovic, you have made a solemn declaration yesterday. You will understand that your testimony today is still in relation to that solemn declaration you made yesterday. Then, Mr. Blaxill, I suppose that you are continuing the interrogation. You may proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I'm much obliged, Mr. President. Your Honours, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Kupusovic, I apologise for going back to one earlier item where I think I should have elicited a little more detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And I beg Your Honours indulgence in that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You referred in your testimony yesterday, Mr. Kupusovic, to a referendum that was held, I believe, at the end of February and early March of 1992. And could you just simply tell what the issue was for which they held that referendum.

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The referendum was held on the 29th of February and the 1st of March, 1992. And the question was: Should Bosnia-Herzegovina become an independent state, or should it remain within Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: What was the result of that referendum?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: More than 67 percent of the population voted in favour of the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Were there any sections or groups in the community who did not take part in the referendum or who had a particular view about it?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The SDS party and its president, Karadzic, called on the Serb people in Bosnia-Herzegovina not to vote in the referendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And do you have any knowledge as to whether that request of Dr. Karadzic was followed by people or not?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was obvious that a part of the Bosnian Serbs did not vote in the referendum, in smaller towns, but also in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Now, Mr. Kupusovic, if I may go back to the point we had reached yesterday. We heard about how the conflict got started in Sarajevo and about the shelling, the sniping, and the conditions that were developing in the city. Was there a time, Mr. Kupusovic, when the action between the forces of the VRS and persons defending the city resulted in establishing some confrontation lines, some formal lines?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The formal lines of defence were established by digging trenches, and this occurred sometime in September and October 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And can you give the Chamber an idea of some of the areas where those lines were actually established?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The lines were mostly established just at the end of the urban part of the city, that is, between the last houses of the town and the woods surrounding the town. And on those woods and slopes were those who were attacking the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Were there any parts of the urban area of Sarajevo that were actually seized and held by the VRS forces?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. With the evacuation of the Marsal Tito barracks in Sarajevo, the part of the town on the left bank of the Miljacka river called Grbavica was under the control of those forces, that is, the army of Republika Srpska, which accounts for about 10 percent of the urban part of the city which was under their control. And they also had control over all the inhabitants around the town -- all the settlements, I'm sorry, around the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: What happened to the area known as Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dobrinja was under a two-fold blockade because it was within the encircled around the town, and the link between Dobrinja and the city itself was constantly exposed to sniping because there was only one road linking the two which could not be used for a long time except at night by driving very quickly around it without stopping.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did that situation subsequently change and Dobrinja become, let's say, more integrated into the city?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First houses were completely destroyed by the fire, so that that communication, that road, became more open to traffic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And about when did that occur?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That occurred at the end of the winter and the beginning of spring of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And I do now want to move, Mr. Kupusovic, if I may, to the year 1993. And what had conditions been over the -- in Sarajevo over the winter, the winter months of 1992 to 1993?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't hear a translation --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I just noticed, Your Honour. I'm not getting a translation either?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we just see if this can be --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It is okay now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please resume at the moment where there was no -- perhaps we should ask the witness -- you should ask the witness to resume his answer to your last question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if you will allow me, in connection with the translation problem, I thought I had understood from what the registrar told us that when a translation problem arises, one should immediately point it out to your Court, your Tribunal. May I ask you, what is the situation now since certain problems have arisen? Should we react each time or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I think if you have a problem with the translation, and as far as I understand, you perhaps can follow the original language of some of the witnesses as well, please react immediately. But of course if it's just the word "a" or "the," if it's not essential, that's -- that has fallen away, perhaps it's not useful to intervene. But if there is any serious problem in translation, you can interfere immediately. But please keep in mind we are not a linguistic society, but we try to understand the witness as he wants to testifies.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, thank you very much for your answer. I will try and do my best to remember that this Tribunal is not as -- to protect languages. I would hope it would be something else. But a small word can have a great meaning. As a simple example, for instance, I have noted in page 58, I think, of -- the witness had said for the exodus of the Serbian people from Sarajevo -- just after having declared that it was essential for military families, Serbian military families, he had declared for the report of the population then was a little more Serbians who had left Sarajevo, which I think I heard. And we can check it on the cassettes, like Malo Vise, "a little more than." The translation - and now I am passing through English for the transcript - does not reflect that idea. It simply gives the idea in writing that there were more Serbians. And I think this sort of distinction is important when you place it back in its context. Page 58 of the transcript of the hearing of the witness yesterday. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do agree with you that small words can have major importance. When it's important, please note immediately. If not, of course we don't have to pay any attention to that. I think about the transcript of yesterday, we can't do anything about that at this moment. But it has been -- it's on the record now that you made -- you clarified an issue that came up yesterday, and we have taken notice of that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I'll go back to the question that I asked before we had a translation problem, and that was I was asking you what were the conditions in Sarajevo over the winter months, between 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In October 1992, supply of the town with electricity was completely stopped. The citizens of Sarajevo and the Presidency of the city had to face a winter during which for some time there would be no electricity. This also meant that there would be no water, because the pumps were running on electric power, and the telephone lines were already out of use. In order to survive, to some extent, in an organised and to a certain extent in a disorganised manner, all the trees that existed in town, in parks and gardens, were cut down for firewood in order to survive the winter. The water supply was organised from old wells of the city brewery, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. and they received fuel from the United Nations forces to be able to run the pumps so that people could go to this spot where the brewery was to collect water. The winter, itself, however, was climate-wise a mild one. But for a large city under siege without power, without water, without city transportation, without any normally functioning utilities, for all these things, alternatives had to be found. Some 10 percent of the city was supplied with gas, natural gas, and many families would get together in those apartments which had gas, and gas was available throughout the winter.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And what about the situation as regards the shelling and the sniping that you've described prior to the winter? How did that go during the wintertime? Was there any difference?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the winter, there were days that were quieter, and there were days with more intensified shelling and sniping. And people were happy when there was a thick fog in town and around it, when there was no sniping.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: During that winter period, and indeed up to that time, how had the emergency services of the city been coping? By that, I mean the fire brigade and the ambulance service.

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both services, considering the conditions, functioned extremely well. Of course, their capacities were reduced because of the shortage of fuel, and they were supplied with fuel with the Red Cross, UNPROFOR, and other international organisations that were operating within the city. And it was very difficult to drive around because of the snow which couldn't be cleared away, so that people mostly went on foot and in sledges.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Were you made aware on the Presidency of any problems directly experienced by the ambulance people and the fire brigade in connection with shelling and sniping?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. On the one hand, they had to respond to these events, but in order to be able to do so, they needed to have the basic supplies, that is, fuel and heating and medical equipment or fire extinguishing equipment. And the role of the Presidency was to intervene constantly with international organisations asking them to help these services which were vital for the survival of the city. And they did assist, that is, the international organisations assisted as much as they could, because their convoys had to pass through barricades and they had to be given permission and be checked out by the forces of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did, to your knowledge, either the ambulance service or the fire service sustain any damage to themselves or their equipment as a result of any shooting?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, many fire brigade vehicles and ambulances were damaged, and their buildings were frequently shelled and exposed to sniping.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: When you refer to buildings, are you referring to the fire brigade or the ambulance service or both?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both. Anyway, all buildings in Sarajevo were under fire, and the building of the emergency service, as the fire brigade building, were directly hit by several shells and were often the target of sniping.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Kupusovic, as we move on to the year 1993, perhaps we can make things a little shorter if I just ask you: Was there any change in the quantity or the frequency of the shelling and the sniping of the city during the course of 1993?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the weather was bad, then we one the impression that the situation was quieter. But generally speaking, there was no change. The city was more or less constantly under sniper fire and shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Were there any times during that year where any form of cease-fire was actually called between the parties?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1993 you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Negotiations were constantly ongoing under the auspices of the United Nations or the European Union, and occasionally agreements were reached on a cease-fire. But these usually lasted five or ten days, and the situation would again deteriorate or return to the situation of constant sniping and shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, during this period, what was the situation regarding hospitals in the city? How many hospitals did they have in Sarajevo during the war?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Sarajevo, there were two large hospitals. And in Dobrinja, there was a provisional hospital, because of this two-fold blockade that I have described.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Could you name the hospitals, please, for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was the clinical centre at Kosevo. This is a large complex of clinics and hospitals. And the state hospital, which was for a time known as the French hospital at Marijin Dvor, the former military hospital. And at Dobrinja, a local dispensary with several doctors who came from the Kosevo clinical centre formed a provisional hospital. It functioned during the war. After the war, it was dismantled.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: The state hospital that you have mentioned, what sort of hospital was that prior to the war?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war, it was the military hospital, and it was used for the needs of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And you made reference to it also being called possibly the French hospital. Could you just explain that, how it acquired that name.

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war, it was a military hospital, and already at the beginning of 1992, in addition to doctors and other medical staff, there were the soldiers and officers of the JNA there. And similarly, to the Marsal Tito barracks, it was a place from which the town was shot at until mid-May. In mid-May, by agreement, all the non-medical and also the medical staff that wanted to leave the hospital was allowed to leave. And immediately after that, the wife of Prime Minister Mitterrand at the time came to Sarajevo and promised the assistance of the French government and the French people for this hospital. That was when a plaque was attached at the entrance to the hospital calling it the French hospital. But because of continued attacks on the city, this hospital didn't really receive a great deal of aid from France, so that it remained as a state hospital under the management of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina formally.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the situation as regards the ability of the Sarajevans during this conflict to bury their dead?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the burial of the dead, the main city cemetery remained outside the encirclement around Sarajevo, and a large cemetery that had been used until the mid-80s, the cemetery at Bare, was very close to the separation lines once they were established, so that neither of these two cemeteries could be used. And then in the town itself, at several locations, temporary burials were organised. However, as this went on too long -- and these cemeteries remain to this day. The Lav cemetery, the stadium at Kosevo that was transformed into a cemetery, and many old cemeteries from the last century were used to bury several dozen or hundreds of newly deceased people.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And were people able to hold normal funeral ceremonies and pay their respects in a way that was like they were able to do before the conflict?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Unfortunately, those sorts of ceremonies and gatherings of people were also a target of attack, shelling and sniping, so that many of these ceremonies had to be stopped and people were very often wounded at the ceremonies themselves. And so they were held late, in the late evening hours or late into the night, when it was possible to bury their dead in greater safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Can you indicate to the Chamber, if you have any idea, as to how many casualities might have resulted in those circumstances?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the course of the whole war in Sarajevo, 12.000 people were killed from the shelling and sniping, and four and a half more -- thousand more people who died of natural causes under the prevailing conditions. So of the 12.000 killed, 1,600 were children.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I see. And those figures you have quoted, do they, in fact, apply to the entirety of the conflict, start to finish?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the entirety of the conflict; from May 1992 up until October 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: As a matter of interest, where did you source that information? Who gave you those figures?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the city of Sarajevo throughout, there was the functioning of an institute for public health. And its job, among other things, was to work with statistical data with respect to health, and of course the citizens of Sarajevo who had died or were killed. The Presidency of the town and also in the newspapers as well, reports would come in daily as to the casualities, the killed, the wounded, and people who had died of some other cause, not from the shelling or sniping. Similarly, the public funeral society, also coming under the authority of the town, and the companies or associations of religious communities for burial also sent out regular reports to the municipal authorities and to the media, newspapers, which were printed during the war in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Of that total figure that you have given us, can you indicate whether those casualities include both military and civilian people?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were the civilian casualities alone. As to the military personnel, we didn't have data on them. But in the town itself, the people who were killed were civilians. Whereas on the front lines, the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. defence lines, where in the course of fighting those casualities were something that the military authorities dealt with because they died as soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Kupusovic, over the period of the conflict, what was the rate of the civilian casualities? Did it in fact -- was it a steady kind of rate of casualities, or were there periods where there were very disparate figures?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course there were periods when there were greater casualities. There were several massacres, in fact; that is to say, situations in which at one and the same time tens of civilians were killed. And there were quieter days, more peaceful days, when in the course of one or two days just one or two people were killed and several wounded and injured. But on an average, that would be 10 or 12 victims, casualities every day over a long period of time, on an average.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So if I say to you in the latter part of 1992, was the casualty rate similar or dissimilar, say, to the first half of 1993?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The numbers were similar, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And what about the second half of 1993 as against the first half of 1993? Again, was this very different or was the rate similar?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think there was a slightly higher number of casualities, but I can't really say. It was more or less the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Would that have applied over the winter of 1993 to 1994?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In the winter of 1993 and the beginning of 1994, I don't know why, but the shooting was intensified, and there were smaller massacres, four or five people at one spot, they would be killed. So there were usually localities where people would go to fetch water or where they would gather to buy bread or things of that kind. And it was most intense prior to the resolution of the United Nations Security Council number 900 in February 1994 when an ultimatum was reached and announced to the forces that had held the town under siege that all their weapons and all snipers and all sniper nests be withdrawn to further away from town, which at the end of February and beginning of March 1994 is what happened. And that is when a peaceful time came to the city of Sarajevo as far as shelling and sniping was concerned. It was a calm period.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Kupusovic, thank you for that. During -- we had been talking about also the conditions in the hospitals. What were the conditions under which the hospitals were working to treat the citizens of Sarajevo, including the casualities of shelling and sniping?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conditions were unbelievably hard. When there was water, then it was the hospitals that had the priority there. But very often they had to do without water. When there was electricity, once again the hospitals would receive the electricity. But very often they had to work by candlelight or generators that they had for emergency surgery. Food, too, was a problem as was heating, and all the other services in the hospital and for the patients, for the injured and wounded, and for the staff as well. It was very difficult to ensure these supplies in a continuous manner. But despite all this, both the hospitals and all the other health centres and clinics were subject to shelling and sniping from time to time, so that the hospitals had to withdraw to the basement areas and to the first and second floors, if we're talking about the former military hospital. From that point of view, Sarajevo was lucky because the hospital capacities and facilities which were built before the war were working for the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but because of the -- the city was under siege, they actually served the city of Sarajevo itself, so they were large. And many parts of the hospital -- the hospitals and the state hospitals were not used, but the capacities were large so that in view of the number of rooms and the staff and personnel, they were fairly successful in contending with the prevailing conditions during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And are you aware - very briefly, if you would - as to whether they encountered any problems over the obtaining of necessary drugs and medicine and medical equipment?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Humanitarian aid, in the form of medicines, were brought in by many humanitarian organisations and the convoys and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: If I could --

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Planes and convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you. If I could move on, Mr. Kupusovic, to the question of the education of the children. How did -- or did anything happen as regards maintaining educational facilities for the children of the city?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The school buildings were full of glass and the glass was shattered, and therefore, the buildings were incapacitated, they couldn't be used, already in May 1992. And so the previous school year was interrupted. And it was only in the autumn of the following year, 1992, in late autumn, in fact, that we were able to organise teaching in basements and secure apartments. We collected the children, gathered the children there with their teachers and started a fresh school year, academic year, under conditions of that kind. The teaching took place once a week or twice a week, so the periods were short. And for the rest of the time, the children had to study with their parents, if they were able to instruct them and give them the education they needed. Many children in that period were evacuated from the city because many humanitarian organisations made offers to have the children evacuated. But of course a lot of children remained in town. And the following year, we were able to print textbooks and notebooks, provisional ones, of course, for the children. We were better able to organise education and teaching. Unfortunately, for all the children, in the first two years of the war, the type of education they received was very poor. And this can be felt in the -- could be felt in the ensuing years. They have great gaps in their education because the education was not continuous. It had, as I said, to take place in the basements and under special conditions, wartime conditions. And the children were taught how to survive and live in the course of the war, whereas the basics that they are usually taught in peace-time, they didn't have time to learn.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Kupusovic, if we move -- you've mentioned the NATO ultimatum that was in February 1994. What effect, if any, did that have on shelling and sniping?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ultimatum, in fact, was to have been implemented by the UNPROFOR command and to control and supervise it, and it did actually take place. It came into being. So at the end of February, or rather, the beginning of March, all the heavy weaponry and the sniper nests and positions were withdrawn. I think they were -- the condition was that they withdraw to within 30 kilometres of the town. And in the city of Sarajevo itself, we saw a period without shelling and without sniping, and this went on until mid-August of that year, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So what, then, happened in mid-August of 1994? And we won't go beyond that date, Mr. Kupusovic. But what then happened in mid-August?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The city was still under siege, but there were no -- there was no sniping or shelling from March to mid-August. We tried to have the city services function slowly, and the United Nations appointed a special representative for the reconstruction of the town's infrastructure. And what we call the Blue Road was opened up via the Mount Igman and the airport, and we were able to communicate with the rest of the country and the world at large. However, on the 17th of August, for reasons that I do not know, there was an attack from the Republika Srpska, a column of vehicles, UN vehicles which were carrying fuel for the town. And they set fire to several tens of vehicles, and that was when the peaceful period and the hope that the people of Sarajevo had that the war had come to an end, at least for them, was buried. That is to say, there was a burgeoning of sniping and shelling once again after August 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Kupusovic, we have heard about the -- we have heard about the problems of water, that valuable resource for the city. When you were on the Presidency, did any particular individual have responsibility for the water supply?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the utilities, water works company that was in charge of the water supply as the main source was behind the line of siege of the city. A commission was set up which incorporated representatives for the other utilities as well, and this commission held negotiations at the airport under the auspices of the UN forces on the establishment of a water supply and electricity supply for the town and with respect to waste waters, and there was a separate commission for military matters and aspects which looked into the security aspects for repairing the main facilities for these systems. I, myself, at that time was a member of the commission for the water supply.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So did you have direct dealings with your Bosnian Serb counterparts in this respect?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Were there occasions you were able to negotiate a supply of water from that original source to the city?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The negotiations took place at the airport under UN auspices whenever it was possible. And on an average, it was possible twice a month, sometimes twice a week.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And how generally did the negotiations go? Did you have any particular difficulties or problems or...

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in principle, there weren't any difficulties because at the negotiations were attended by people whose job that was. So from the very beginning, they said that water, electricity, and the other utilities will no longer -- would no longer be used to terrorise the citizens of Sarajevo. And then we looked into the technical feasibilities of having 10 to 20 percent of capacities put into operations straight away. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. And that's what usually happened. But after a few days or weeks, there was an interruption again, a breakdown. And after a few weeks of negotiation, we were able to establish the supply source again. And that's how it went throughout the winter of 1993 up until the -- the war effects on Sarajevo were discontinued at the beginning of 1994

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You've used an expression there of using the water or electricity to terrorise the citizens. Can you tell us a little bit more about that, I mean as to what you mean by using the -- those utilities in that fashion.

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Sarajevo, the citizens themselves were exposed to terrorisation, that is to say, a constant pressure that they could not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Blaxill, Mr. Piletta-Zanin would like to interfere.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm very sorry to have to intervene. If I have to hear what the witness is saying. I think that the microphone doesn't work well at all. I can't hear properly a translation and listen to another and hear what the witness is saying. It should be possible to raise the volume of the microphone so that I could have my ear free to listen. I cannot follow what the witness is saying. It's purely a technical matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll discuss this with my colleagues and see what technically can be done about it. On the other hand, of course, a human being has some limitations in hearing. You haven't even got three ears to follow three languages. Do I understand well, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, that you would like to have the level of the volume of the sound in the courtroom a bit higher so that with one ear you can listen to the translation and with the other to the original language spoken?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not exactly, Mr. President. I'm trying to get a translation in one ear, to follow another one, and to listen to what the witness is saying. And in order to be able to listen to what he is saying, one should raise the volume in the room. Yes, in the room. I have understood. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just ask the technicians whether it's possible to have the higher level of sound in the courtroom but of course not so loud that we'll be disturbed by the sound in the courtroom. I do understand that this is not possible. So I'll just ask you at least to have your best ear in the courtroom and the other ear on the earphones. We tried, but we can't effect it. Thank you. Mr. Blaxill, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I'm obliged to you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Kupusovic, I had asked you if you could expand a little on what you mean by the use of the water system and the electricity as ways of terrorising the population of Sarajevo. And if you could clarify what you mean by that.

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We -- all of us in Sarajevo knew that the siege of Leningrad in the Second World War lasted for 1.000 days, or rather, 900 days, but that the water supply was not used as a purpose to attain one's wartime goals. For Sarajevo, water was used as a means to render citizens' lives impossible. And at the negotiations that I mentioned that were held at the airport, when we -- the two sides had tete-a-tete meetings, that is, the representatives of the city on the one side and those who were around the town on the other. They said that the water would no longer be used as a means to attain war goals. But then, for example, when it came to repairing a pump, they put it off for a week or two, so it took a week or two to have the water flowing. And then a valve was closed off, and there wasn't any more water. The representatives of the United Nations who were acting as mediators, only towards the end of the war were they allowed by the army of Republika Srpska to be on the spot, to be where the pumps were, and the electricity stations so as to be able to ensure that they were not used as a means of war. So throughout that time, later on, they were -- they served citizens. They would give out small quantities, then break them off. And this was cyclic. But it had a very hard effect on the population because they lost the meaning of life, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you. Just, perhaps, to state the obvious in a way, where was the ultimate control of the water supply situated? In whose territory?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the territory controlled by the forces of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Where was the ultimate control of the electricity supply situated? On whose territory?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The electricity supply -- there were 11 transformer stations around the city, and they were all under the control of the forces of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Are you aware as to whether water lines to the city or the piping ever received damage from shelling or sniping-type damage?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main pipeline was never damaged, but the local distribution network was damaged here and there, but not by shells directly but, rather, due to the rapid changes in the amount of air and water in those pipes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Kupusovic, I just wish to move now, if I may, sir, to my last topic for discussion with you, and that is this: Throughout all the events that you have been describing yesterday and today, what was the effect psychologically on yourself and on your fellow citizens, your fellow Sarajevans who were in that city?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As Sarajevans, we experienced our first shock on the 2nd of May when the war actually began in Sarajevo, that is, the siege and the shelling. Throughout those first few months, we thought that the war must come to an end by the following week, that what was happening was quite impossible. However, that didn't happen. And in October 1992, when the town was left without any electricity at all, this was another psychological shock, and we wondered whether it was possible to survive at all under those circumstances. Because the bakery had the flour, but if there's no electricity, it couldn't make bread. And if there's no water, that is, pumped by electricity, again, it cannot produce bread. The cease-fires or the interruptions in the attacks on the town gave hope that the situation would gradually improve, but after each of those cease-fires, shelling would resume with even greater intensity, as well as sniping, and then people psychologically started to lose faith and hope that they would be able to survive at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Can I interrupt you there for a moment, sir. Can you say what - very specifically you've made reference now to shelling and sniping - what specific emotions that you observed in yourself and others were created by the fact of the shelling and of the sniping that was done on the civilians of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, I am not an expert. But I know, judging by my children and my friends, the psychological reaction was that we had to somehow get away from that town. And the people who had firmly decided to leave were taken by convoys and even by UN planes and transported to countries that were willing to receive refugees from Bosnia and Herzegovina, so that 100.000 pre-war citizens of Sarajevo left the town during the first and second year of the war. I have already mentioned that quite a number of children were evacuated. But also, various other groups of people had left the city. And for those who remained, they did so because that was their town. They stayed behind either because they had obligations towards their family, but the psychological effect was most depressing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Kupusovic, can you perhaps describe to me the feelings you might have when you had to step out of your house in Sarajevo to go and fetch something? What sort of emotions did you recall in yourself, and you maybe noticed amongst friends, when you were faced with having to go out on the streets?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One had to go out either to fetch bread or water, or simply because you couldn't spend all your time in the basement or the safer part of your apartment. And for the people who stayed behind, there was fear whether the person who went out would come back alive or wounded, and also the person going out wondered, as soon as he hears a shell, whether his apartment had been hit. And this was terrible fear because you couldn't communicate with anyone by telephone. And if you hear that there had been sniping or shelling somewhere, then immediately you think of your children or your wife or family. Until you get together again, you are under terrible stress. And this was something that happened regularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: May I interrupt you there. I'm sorry to do so, Mr. Kupusovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe there is an error in transcript my learned friend has pointed out to me. There is a reference at line 19, page 22 that refers to hundreds of civilians left the town during the second year of the war. Our recollection is that the expression was hundreds of thousands. I see His Honour Judge Nieto Navia is nodding agreement. We believe, also - I'm sorry, I wasn't paying adequate attention to the script myself at that point - it was, "Between the first and second year, hundreds of thousands of people ..." I believe the reference in the transcript is simply "the second year". Perhaps I could re-ask those questions for absolute clarity. Would it assist Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you would please do so, so that it will not Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. be necessary later on to change the transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Kupusovic, because of the situation with the transcript, you mentioned the numbers of people who had left the city. And the record showed it was in the second year and hundreds of civilians. Now, could you just recall what you actually said or meant in that regard as to the numbers of people who left the city and when they did?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant to say that in the first two years of the war, 100.000 citizens left the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I think that is now eminently clear, Your Honour. I'll proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kupusovic, could we go back. You said that you referred to the stress and the thoughts of your family and so forth when you went out and around in the city. Is there anything further you can say about the mental effects of the sniping and the shelling upon you or other Sarajevans such as perhaps have you any lasting effects from that experience? Have you noticed any behavioural things in others or yourself that reflect that psychological experience?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that everyone who experienced the war in Sarajevo has lasting effects. But for me personally and my immediate family, we have endeavoured to put it behind us. This happened. Thank God, we have physically survived, and focussing on today and tomorrow, we manage to live with these mental scars from that period. There were very many cases of children coming back after the war where they had been refugees. And when they met with the children who had stayed in Sarajevo, these encounters between the two groups showed a lack of understanding between them. The same applies to adults, but somehow they seek to deal with that better. But anyway, there are very few people outside Sarajevo who can understand those who lived through it in Sarajevo. But, of course, the Sarajevans who were refugees did not have an easy time either, but at least they were not exposed to shelling and sniping and shortage of basic food stuffs as well as electricity and water. Personally, and my colleagues at work also, looking to the future, we are living with this past of ours, which should remain in the past. And those who are to blame for that should be held accountable by this Tribunal and punished.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Kupusovic, I thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And Mr. President, Your Honours, that does conclude my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Blaxill. It's now the Defence has the opportunity to cross-examine Mr. Kupusovic. But perhaps I would first like to know how much time do you think you'll need for cross-examination, if you want to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you. It is our estimate that we will need about two hours for the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You understand I am looking at the clock. Perhaps it would be -- so we have approximately a bit over -- two hours left. Perhaps it would be better to make a break now, if this is possible, for the technical support and the interpretation, and then start cross-examination. So I would say -- I have some difficulties in looking at the clock because there's a lot of reflection. But if we would start at 4.00, is that all right with you, Ms. Pilipovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you. But I would like, before I start my cross-examination, to address the question of tendering of evidence which you raised yesterday, but we didn't discuss it. Since my learned friends from the Prosecution had not intended to tender this document, the Defence in the cross-examination would like to tender to the Court certain documents into evidence. For technical reasons, I would like to know how we will be dealing with this tendering of documents. And with your leave, I can tell you that we have prepared five copies of text from two books in the B/C/S and English language. Is that sufficient, I wonder? So could we deal with that now, and then have our break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One moment, please, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, I understand that during a pre-trial 18 meeting with the management, an arrangement has been made that seven copies of each document should be provided by the parties when they tender exhibits in evidence. And the second thing is they should be pre-numbered. Are they pre-numbered according to what has been arranged for, these exhibits? Otherwise, if everybody is all right and there's no problem, we proceed just as we arranged. If there is still some problem, perhaps you could use the half-hour break to have the number of copies we would like to have and the numbering being completed. Could you please tell us whether the preparation in this respect is done?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you very much. It just means that I need another two copies, and that's why I just asked so that there would be no problems later on when tendering the documents. Thank you very much. So this break will come in very handy for me to make another two copies, so I will have seven. And also, I will pre-number them 1, 2, and 3, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And as far as I understand, it's the practice in this Court that you can use these exhibits without -- we expect once you show an exhibit to a witness, that you'll tender them in evidence. If there's any objection against a document from the other party, please raise this objection immediately. But if there's no objection, then we can have these exhibits tendered and admitted in evidence at the end of the testimony of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Understood, Your Honour. The only thing is at this point in time, we are unaware of these documents and their contents. I think we could profitably use the break period to look into the matter, and perhaps if there is any further comment from the Prosecution, perhaps we could make that comment on conclusion of the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's fine. We will have a break until 4.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, you have been able to make a couple of copies extra.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Your Honour. Everything is in order now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the Prosecution now aware of the exhibits that will be used during the cross-examination, and is there any comment on the material that will be used?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: The answer to both your questions, Mr. President, is yes. We have the documents. We are aware of their contents. The Prosecution has no objection to the practice of a cross-examining party putting a document to a witness, with a view to it then being entered into evidence subsequent to that cross-examination. But, however, our observation is that we feel there has to be a need for a proper evidential foundation for a given document to be put to a witness. In other words, the document must have some kind of relevance to that witness's testimony or experience so that they could properly use the witness as a vehicle for the given document. So it is subject to that qualification that there be a proper evidential foundation why it should go through that witness. Other than that, we have no objection to the practice, quite clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So let's just start the procedure. And if it comes to -- ever to any document that might not be linked to the witness, then we'll see what happens, and perhaps you could then respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Well, we would propose perhaps offering any comment from the Prosecution side -- at the point where my learned friend wanted to tender the document, then we would make any challenge that was appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course, unless there are other reasons to challenge the evidence to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: The unforeseen or whatever, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then Ms. Pilipovic, we will ask the witness to come in, and you then may cross-examine the witness. Or is it Mr. Piletta-Zanin who is going to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if you will allow me, I think that it is essential that the Defence may just before the cross-examination may call the attention of your Tribunal, if possible with the documents, on certain facts which give back to the Defence the rights -- makes the exercise of its rights very difficult, if not impossible. But I only need one minute to explain what the Defence has to do tomorrow before the cross-examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I suggest -- you say "what has to do tomorrow before the cross-examination of the witness." That's what I read on my transcript. One minute to explain. Tomorrow, before the cross-examination of the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But we thought at the time that the cross-examination would be tomorrow, you see. Now it's going to be today. And it's just before this hearing on the cross-examination that we would like to submit these matters to the Tribunal for a few seconds, a few short seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, first of all, I expect every party to be Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. prepared at least a couple of hours in advance if things go a bit quicker. We have to be prepared for that. That's my first observation. If there's one thing at this moment you would like to bring under the attention of the Chamber, you could do it, but don't use all the time you would have otherwise have used for cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you so much, Mr. President. We will use this time which could be taken on our time for cross-examination, but I really think it's necessary to be able to express ourselves now. What I wanted to say, Mr. President, Your Honours, is simply that we received a few hours only ago -- only a few hours ago, and only one of the two counsel for the Defence, about 97 folders which are not in this room, this courtroom - I can't see them here. I suppose nobody dared bring them in - 87 folders where you have all the exhibits, and in particular some of the exhibits which would particularly be interesting for the cross-examination. In order to help us in this demarche, it was furnished to the Defence, a search engine which could also help the Tribunal to retrieve necessary data in this -- data, which a few hours ago, about 41.757 pages -- 41.757 pages by the search engine, we can only find 37 documents which contain or incorporate the name of General Galic. In these 37 documents, more than half are newspaper clips, articles, press commentaries, stories which have absolutely no direct connection or immediate connection with the facts. And another 30 seconds if I may, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I would like to interrupt you at this moment, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. I feel that you are pointing at certain shortcomings in the documents you have been provided by the Prosecution. And I know that this has been an issue before, and I suggest that we discuss this matter at a Status Conference which will be held immediately after the examination of the witness, and I also suggest to you that if new documents have come up, and overnight you might have new thoughts on them, and if you can show the relevance of your remarks for the examination of Mr. Kupusovic, then you come up with this specific point even before the Status Conference. But the other issues, numbers of documents, relevance of documents, we will discuss that I think better during the Status Conference. If you would agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, thank you very much. I have no other choice than to accept. But it would be necessary to say very clearly - and we can talk about it tomorrow - one should say very clearly that we are not in a position to cross-examine in an efficient way this witness for reasons I wanted to explain, which I think you were not able to hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I just read the transcript on the last line. These new documents -- it would be unfair to finish cross-examination of the witness without these documents. We will come back to that later. And you have an opportunity to use these documents when relevant in any further state of the proceedings. So I would now like to ask the usher to bring in the witness, Mr. Kupusovic, and I'll give you the opportunity to cross-examine Mr. Kupusovic. You may proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kupusovic, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Before I start with my questions, I should like you to confirm for us that for the past couple of years, you have been cooperating with the Tribunal investigators, that on the 22nd and 23rd of May, 1996 you made a statement as a witness. Can you confirm that, please? Is that true?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact dates, but I did give statements in 1996 and appeared in this Tribunal as a witness that same year.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You were a witness in case IT-95-18, on the 1st of July, 1996?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I am not familiar with the numbers you're referring to, but I was a witness concerning the same matter, that is, the situation in Sarajevo in the proceedings against Karadzic and Mladic in their absence.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: On the 2nd of February and the 26th of October, 2000, you had an interview with the investigators of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on two occasions. I don't remember the exact dates, but probably you are right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: As Defence counsel, I have those documents in my possession, and I just wanted you to confirm that you had those conversations with our learned friends from the Prosecution. On 13th of November and the 1st of December, you also had an interview with the Prosecution investigators.

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the course of the examination-in-chief by my learned friends, you said that you were a professor at the university and director of an institute. Will you tell us when you became a university professor and when director of the institute. What year?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I worked at the university every since my graduation in 1977; and as senior assistant, I became in 1988; and in 1990, I became director of the institute for hydro engineering attached to the civil engineering department of the university.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that you lived at Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Will you please tell us what part of Dobrinja was your apartment. In what part of Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is called Dobrinja I, next to the road. And across the road is the runway of Sarajevo airport.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: As you have told us that it was Dobrinja I, does that mean that in that part of the settlement, there are several Dobrinja settlements with different numbers?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first part of Dobrinja that was built in 1983, and that is why it was called Dobrinja I. And there are also Dobrinja II, III IV, and also I think V. In fact it is all one settlement, but the numbers were given consecutively as they were built.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: What municipality did the Dobrinja residential area belong to?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It belonged to the municipality called Novi Grad, or "new city."

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that the airport was close to where you lived. Could you tell us, in view of the fact that you were born in Sarajevo and you were living in Sarajevo, what is in the immediate vicinity and in the surroundings of Dobrinja? Are there other settlements or certain hills or other features?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the one side is the main road going from Stup to Kula. And on the right-hand side of the road is the airport, and on the left-hand side the settlement of Dobrinja. In the direction of Lukavica, there is the barracks, the JNA barracks. And on the opposite from the airport is Brdo, and the hill is called Mojmilo, and that is where the water reservoir is. As you're heading towards the centre of the city is the Nedzarici district and Ali Pasino Polje district.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And Igman mountain?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mount Igman is on the other side of the airport. There's Dobrinja, then the airport, then railway tracks, then some other settlements, and then Mount Igman. So from my window, I could see both the airport and Mount Igman looking in the same direction.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: To avoid repetition, you told us what the municipalities of Sarajevo were. Could you tell us what the composition of the population was in the various municipalities?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you offhand, by it was roughly the same as for the whole of the city, which I've already said: 40 percent Muslim, 30 percent Serbs, 8, 9 percent Croats, and the rest were those who were mixed. In Dobrinja, there was a particularly high percentage of mixed marriages because it was a new settlement, so that in every building, there were families of different ethnicities.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know which of the municipalities in which the Serb population had a majority?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not predominant in any single municipality, but in the old district of Nedzarici, as far as I know, there were more Serbs than others. But this is because this used to be a village, and then when it became a part of the city, it was an area where there were more Serbs. And then the same applies to Stup, which was a suburb, or rather, village where Croats were more numerous, and later it was integrated into the city. And the people living there remained majority Croats. There were other Muslim villages also that became part of the city where the Muslims were more numerous than others.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In relation to all those municipalities, the ten municipalities that constituted the city of Sarajevo, where were the economic resources, the large companies in Sarajevo? Could you tell us in which part of the city they were situated?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were all over town. Sarajevo, with its ten municipalities, was administratively organised in such a way that the larger factories should be in the suburbs, such as, Hranici, Pale, Korin [phoen], Hadzici, Vogosca, and other settlements. And in the town itself, the urban part of the city, we had mostly the premises of consulting and designing companies. There were very few factories in the town itself but -- left over from the last century, but mostly commercial firms, and of course the city's infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that you were a member of the SDA party. When did you become a member? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just before the elections in 1990. I joined at the end of August. And the elections took place in November.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When was the SDA party formed?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in March 1990.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Before that, were you a member of any other party?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that you headed the SDA list at the elections. Could you tell us whether you were an official in the SDA party and what was your function?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the elections nor after the election was I an SDA official, but I was the head of the list. I was proposed to head the list by the party officials as a respected citizen born in Stari Grad for which I headed the list. After several assembly meetings in 1990, I was elected president of the SDA club of deputies in the city assembly, and as such, I did participate in certain party meetings. But I was no party official. I was not a party official.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that three national parties were formed, that is, the parties in Sarajevo, the SDA, the HDZ, and the SDS. Could you tell us the order in which they were formed?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, the SDA was the first to be formed, then the HDZ, and after that, the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did interethnic relations deteriorate in Sarajevo after the formation of those parties?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: No. When did the relations deteriorate?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the whole of Sarajevo, they did not at all until the war. But in the whole of Bosnia and Herzegovina, later those relations deteriorated.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Which party won at the elections in Sarajevo? Which was the leading party?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a single party in Sarajevo got an absolute majority, but in the city assembly in which I participated, the SDA had a relative majority, 42 deputies out of a total of 120, which means 31 or 32 per cent; whereas the SDS had 28 percent, and the HDZ, 4. And the other four parties elected to the assembly had between 1 and 2 deputies to 22 deputies in the city assembly.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: How did that assembly function and until when did it function?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The assembly functioned very well in my opinion until March of 1992, and then it didn't function for two years, and then it resumed in March 1994 until after the Dayton Peace Agreements, and after that as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: After the conflict broke out in Sarajevo, a Presidency was formed, you told us. Could you explain in somewhat greater detail the role of that Presidency.

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're probably referring to the city Presidency of which I was a member. It was formed on the basis of the constitution and the law because the assembly was unable to meet, that is, all 120 deputies, or rather, a two-thirds majority of that number, that is, 81 deputies. In April, it was unable to meet, and then at the beginning of June the Presidency was formed, which took over all the competences of the assembly, that is, the highest civilian authority in Sarajevo for the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that on the 4th of April, 1992, an immediate threat of war or state of war was proclaimed in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Was it officially proclaimed then, I don't remember. But that is what it was, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And when was a general mobilisation called?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later, in mid-May.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: But you will agree with me that the functions of the Presidency were a wartime Presidency of the assembly of Sarajevo; however, mobilisation was called by the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did that War Presidency function on the basis of the principle of crisis staffs?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. According to the laws taken over from the [Realtime transcript read in error "SFOR"] SFRY, it consisted the town mayor, the deputy town mayor, a lady, the head of civil defence, the head of the local police, and representatives of political parties who were elected to the city assembly. So that the Presidency was composed of members of different parties and different people of different ethnicity and different political views, but people who sought to make life in town possible, in the civilian sense.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So that War Presidency was formed in June 1992?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I've noticed that at line 25, page 37, it said "according to the laws taken over from the SFOR." That is, in fact, SFRY. I do recall hearing that. And it's a significant difference because SFOR was an acronym for one of the UN presidencies in Bosnia, currently even.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that's the recollection of my colleagues, as well as it is mine, so it must be a typing mistake at this moment. It's also quite logical it's not the SFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Indeed. Apologies otherwise.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can we ask counsel and witness to pause between questions and answers, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm asked whether a short pause could be made between the question and the answers to be given. Mr. Kupusovic, if you would look at the screen, and perhaps look at when it stops moving, that's where the interpretation and the transcript is at a point where they can proceed. And if you would wait until that moment before answering the question, yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Yes, I'll bear that in mind, Your Honour. Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You spoke to us about the referendum. Can you tell us who organised the referendum in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The referendum was organised by the government of the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or rather, the decision for a referendum was made by the assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to know whether the decision by that assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina was in conformity with the BH constitution that was in force at the time?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was in conformity with the prevailing constitution and the procedure for decision-making applicable in the assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When they took the decision for a referendum at the BH assembly, did the deputies of Serb ethnicity take part as well?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did take part, but the deputies of the SDS party withdrew from the assembly meeting when it came to a vote on the referendum.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Will you agree with me that that was the reason why the referendum was in fact boycotted, the fact that the Serb deputies did not take part in the work of the assembly?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the referendum was boycotted because of the appeal made by Radovan Karadzic to sympathisers of the SDS not to come out to the referendum. That's what I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: At that referendum for independence, did a two-thirds vote, or more than two-thirds or less than two-thirds?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: More than two-thirds voted of the voters listed, and the vast majority, 99 point something of those who went out to vote, voted in favour of Bosnia and Herzegovina's independence under the prevailing conditions when the referendum -- on the day the referendum was held.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday during your examination-in-chief you read out a statement, and can you tell me how the idea was reached and the reasons for making this statement of the 17th of April, I believe it was?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation around the referendum and the negotiations between the presidents of the three national parties took place at a republican level. In the town itself, we followed this process and endeavoured to define the town's position vis-a-vis what was happening at the level of Bosnia-Herzegovina and with the outside world, so that of all the presidents of the clubs, quite spontaneously, at a meeting that we held to see what we could do as a city, the idea was reached to sign a statement of that kind, by which we demonstrated, or wanted to demonstrate to the citizens, that their representatives, elected representatives, publicly, both for Sarajevo and for Bosnia-Herzegovina, and for the whole world, were striving for a united city which would respect its age-old heritage and values. And the important thing was that all the parties agreed, the representatives of all the parties, and that is how we wrote that statement and published it in the media and on television and over the radio.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Was one of the reasons the fact that the internationality relations in the city of Sarajevo were upset?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were not upset, and a statement of this kind confirmed that, because it was signed precisely by -- that is to say, in its creation, we had the participation of all the national and other parties. Now, whether at the level of Bosnia-Herzegovina relations had been disrupted, because certain autonomous regions, Serbian and otherwise, had already been proclaimed, so there were some proposals from the peaks of the SDS about the division of the city into ethnic regions or districts, which was not possible for Sarajevo, and completely unacceptable, of course. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: After the referendum that was held on the 29th and the 1st in Sarajevo, were there any significant manifestations or rallies or expressions of any particular positive or negative thoughts by the citizens? Was there any positive or negative thinking on the part of the citizens, and was this manifest in the streets?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both in the streets and in the work of the town in general, there were positive thoughts, as you said a moment ago, that they would not follow the pattern of the events of Bijeljina or other towns in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that we would not be precipitous in that. And there were peace movements that were emerging and initiatives to have Sarajevo as the centre of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the symbol of Bosnia-Herzegovina, not to be drawn into something like that, as happened in Vukovar or Dubrovnik, for example, or in other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina, not to be pulled in in that way, where crisis staffs had been set up, the ones which you mentioned, and which were based on an ethnic affiliation and which led later on to the war that was to come for several years.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us something about the events of the 1st of March, 1992, which happened in Bascarsija?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you anything about that, because I wasn't there, or anywhere in the surroundings. There were different interpretations by the press as to what had actually happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: What was in the press? What did the papers say about the event?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a wedding, and there was an incident that broke out. Now, what actually happened, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did the paper say that it was the first civilian to be killed in Sarajevo, that he was a Serb, and that he was killed by a Musan Topalovic, Caco, who was later the commander of a unit in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hear that for the first time from you here and now, that it was Musan Topalovic who performed that act. Actually, I don't know what happened myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to know at that particular time in Sarajevo - and when I say "that time," I'm thinking of March and April, because you started speaking about the months of March and April - that paramilitary units existed, that is to say, units which were called the Green Berets and the Patriotic League?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have also mentioned the groups that were called Bosna, and under that heading we would include the Green Berets and others. They were groups of self-organised young men, along with the reserve police formations, or within the police force themselves, belonging to the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They were not wearing uniforms, or neither were they equipped, so in that sense they could have been paramilitary, but they were not organised as any party or other kind of army. Quite simply, there was fear as to what could happen. There were several thousand people around the 2nd of May that started calling themselves the Green Berets or the Bosna Group, and similar groups.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So according to you, in March and April, nothing happened in Sarajevo; is that right? Why, then, would the Green Berets have been established, and other paramilitary formations or units, if I can call them that?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when they were formed. I think they had already been formed earlier on. Now, I know some people who took part in them said that they had been actually established earlier on. I heard about them for the first time sometime in March and April, and I can't tell you anything more about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
