utterances.text: Do you happen to know that the Patriotic League was a party army of the SDA party, in fact, and that it was established at the level of the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina with units, that units had existed since 1991, in fact?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't tell you for the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but I know for Sarajevo for sure; I know that no units of the Patriotic League of any kind existed, nor did the Patriotic League -- nor was it an organised formation in any way. I lived there, and I was even in the assembly and places like that in town. What the SDA did there, I don't really know. But what I took part in, I have already explained and described. And in the part where I was, there was never anything about those units. I don't know about them. But later on in May, when the Territorial Defence grew to become the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I had heard that there was a patriotic league of some kind or groups which had some emblems of a democratic league but in fact they became the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to know the names of Juka Prazina, Ramiz Delalic, Celo, Musan Topalovic, Caco, and Ramiz Salcin? Can you tie the formation of those units to those names?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know the names very well, just as all the other citizens of Sarajevo do. Now, as to linking up those names or those people with the units, I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, were the media working in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, television was working, when there was electricity. Yes, the media were functioning.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: What about when there was no electricity? Could you follow television and the rest of the media?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you had batteries, you could listen to your radio. Television had a news broadcast, in the evening hours, televised a news bulletin. So if there was electricity, then you could watch. If not, you couldn't. You would have to rely on your radio and batteries if you had them.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When there was electricity and when the media were functioning, were you able to follow the activities of those military units on television, on the television programme in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up until October 1992, we did have electricity, and were therefore able to watch television and follow the events in Bosnia-Herzegovina and in the world, of course, linked to Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Does the name Kerim Loncarevic, nicknamed "doctor" ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kerim Loncarevic was a colleague, a deputy in the municipal assembly, so I do know the name, yes. I know him. And he is in Sarajevo now.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that he wrote a book?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that he had a military unit, military police unit of his own?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that for a time, he was the commander of a -- of the military police and the staff of the Supreme Command of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. He didn't have his own unit. His unit was a part of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina of which he was a commander at that particular time, that is to say, the second half of 1992 and until some time in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to know that in 1992, in March and April, he was the leader of a paramilitary formation which had its soldiers and that their headquarters were in Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I lived in Dobrinja at the time, and there were no military or paramilitary units except for the JNA in the barracks and at the airport.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence would like to show the witness a text taken from a book written by Kerim Loncarevic. The book was published in Sarajevo, and the title is "The Battle for Sarajevo." And in the book, he describes the events in 1992. And it was printed on the 12th of April, 2000, "Destined for Victory" is the other title of the book. With your permission, and subject to my learned colleagues' agreement, I should like to have the witness shown a passage, a short passage taken from that book. And I should like to ask the witness to comment on the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, perhaps I could indicate to the Court that out of the three names given a moment ago by Ms. Pilipovic, only one was mentioned in the transcript, and I think the three names should be repeated perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps, Ms. Pilipovic, if you would please repeat these names and then spell them out so that there can be no misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Juka Prazina, Aramas Daramiccelo [phoen], Musan Topalovic, Caco, Ramiz Salcin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please now check in the transcript whether the names are there in an acceptable spelling.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see in the transcript that the names have not been recorded properly. With your permission, we shall write down the names and give them to the court reporters for them to enter them into the transcript properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You have before you a text, and it's the 76th page, page 76, taken from the book "The Battle for Sarajevo." And on page 76, could you read the sentence that begins with, "I had previous designated the critical spots, locations, in town ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Your Honours, I fear I have to object to this point. As I understand it, it has not been established that this witness knows this author and this book or anything of that nature, and further, that he has indicated he has already stated that he knew nothing of paramilitaries or these people's names in connection with Dobrinja. So I'm wondering that -- it is improper, I would suggest, that he should now read any section of this material into the record of the transcript of the Tribunal in circumstances where it's not been established that you have Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. any knowledge of the subject about which he has been asked to read outloud.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll just confer with my colleagues for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As far as the objection of the Prosecution is concerned - first I have to find my earphones - we would prefer if Ms. Pilipovic would agree that he reads this part of the book. There's no discussion about whether this is a part of the book, I understand, or is there any discussion about it? She reads it to the witness, and then can ask any question about whether this brings something into his mind, which is of course possible. And it's not a final answer that he has given now. It has not been much many detail, in general terms. So Ms. Pilipovic, if you would be willing to read the part yourself in the original and then ask questions about it to the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I had previously designated the critical locations in town. I believe my fighters -- my fighters were in Dobrinja. Brijesce and Buljakov Potok was Smajo Sukalo [phoen]. Smajo was there with the intervention platoon unit. At Kosevsko Polje, there was Dzilda with a complete unit. Ramiz Salcin was in Svrakino Selo. The intervention unit of Tabija was at Vratnik. Igor with the MGM was at Ali Pasino Polje. Zoran with the mambes was in the C-phase of Ali Pasino Polje. The command of the military police with three onslaught intervention units was at Bjelave. Topa was at the national bank. Celo was at Vrbanja bridge. Ejup at Koblija Glava. And Ramiz was protecting Vratnik with his fighters. Tiab with his intervention unit was at the brewery. Delta with the Aljic brothers was in Velesici. My brother Zuti did not go from Otoka. Can we defend occupied Sarajevo? Can we stand up to the tanks that are about to leave the barracks?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Your Honours, before my learned friend asks questions of the witness I do note there are certain areas where the translation that we have does not entirely accord with what has been now translated to us as my learned friend has been reading. And I suppose the most significant of those is that there was mention particularly of somebody was -- well, I'm afraid the names are missing from the transcript. But there was somebody there with a complete unit, and that particular reference is totally missing from our translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters apologise, but they did not have a copy of the translation or the text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The translator tells me they did not have a copy beforehand. Perhaps this is not even bad because we now see that there can be some differences. Could you please point exactly -- perhaps in relation to any name where there was a difference of translation so that we can clarify this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Grant me a moment if you would, Mr. President. Well the particular reference I have, if you look at the transcript, Your Honour, is at line 20 on page 47 of the transcript. It's towards the upper third of the screen. And there was the very specific reference to somebody being there with a complete unit, and I recall that that certainly is not in the translation of this passage that was actually handed to us by the Defence at the commencement of the break. This was their translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Pilipovic, this is approximately the third -- it's right in the beginning of the text. And since there are some difficulties in translation, I would like to clarify it. I would just look at my other screen. You translated "My fighters were in Dobrinja." That's the second line. Then a couple of names are missing with -- when it comes to with the intervention platoon unit, intervening unit. And then I think we have got three names, Ramiz was in Svrakino Selo -- could you please read in translation the second part of the third line and the first part of the fourth line, perhaps in the English translation. You read some English, or perhaps you could be assisted by your colleague. Yes? He nods no, but you say yes. So I keep you to your spoken word. Could you please take this part again so that we see that there's a proper translation about the complete unit. Some person with a complete unit. Is this right or wrong in the translation, and perhaps you could ask the translators to look at the original text. Have they got an original text?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters have not been provided with the original text.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, could you provide the interpreters with the original text because that's really necessary to sort this out.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is precisely what I was going to propose to the Tribunal, to give the original text to the interpreters so a complete reading can be given out of this text so it would be much more simple.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please take care of that when you produce another text, that there are originals always available for the interpreters' booth. This is a matter of order.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I've taken note of it personally, Mr. President, and also my colleague personally, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I tried to identify the exact place what we are discussing about, and that is the line that is immediately followed by the sentence that begins with Ramiz. So could you please read in the original text the sentence preceding the sentence that begins with Ramiz. I think it starts with something like "in Brijesce". Read it, and then we have it translated by the interpreters in the booth, and then we'll see whether we can agree on that translation. Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in the fifth row, I have the beginning of a sentence beginning with "Ramiz Salcin".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, in the translation, it's the third line. So the sentence preceding the line that begins with "Ramiz Salcin". I think it's the second sentence of the text you ...

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At Kosevsko Brdo, there was Dzilda with a complete unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that's what you translated, the complete unit. It's in our translation, it's different. It says in Brijesce and Buljakov Potok was Smajo Sukalo [phoen] with the intervening unit. Would you agree that the translation as given by the interpreters is a correct one?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, then that's the translation we rely upon. Thank you. You may proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kupusovic, I have read out the text from this book on page 76. You spoke to us yesterday about tanks leaving the barracks. Can you agree with me that these units and these young men opposed the tanks which, as they put it, should have left the barracks?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read this out carefully, and I've already said, here it says that at Dobrinja, the author says "My fighters were there. I lived in Dobrinja and there were no units at Dobrinja except for JNA units around Dobrinja, at he airport and at the Mojmilo water reservoir." There were tanks coming out of the barracks in February and in March and in April 1992. And those were allegedly exercises by the JNA, and nobody opposed them. As for the other units, I know nothing about them. You will probably put that question to the Witness, the author of this book.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that you eyewitnessed the events of the 2nd of May, 1992 when from the Marsal Tito barracks, soldiers with tanks were coming out. You told us that a conflict broke out, that in that fighting, among others, some young men had taken part. Would you allow the possibility for these young men and these units to have resisted the tanks?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the special forces of the MUP and the reserve police force and maybe these young men, if you want to put to that way, there were some other young men in addition to these, who belonged to the armed formations of Bosnia-Herzegovina, therefore, the police, who resisted, because they were in the city assembly. And from the windows, they told me they could see tanks approaching the Presidency building, which is next door to this building. And that is where the clash occurred. I, myself, was actually in the street. I was an eyewitness seeing the tanks opening fire at the Presidency and the city assembly, and fire was returned from those buildings against those tanks. But let me correct myself: As far as I know, they didn't come out of the Marsal Tito barracks, but rather, from Lukavica, and they came from the other side of the Miljacka river.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Was this a column with soldiers in it?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. They were armoured transportors, APCs, a column of some 10 or 15 or more vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who was in that column as you were an eyewitness?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: JNA vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that your president was in that column, Alija Izetbegovic? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember whether that was that very event, because there was another situation when the column in which the president of the Presidency was in - Izetbegovic - returning from the negotiations in Lisbon, he was captured, he spent the night in the barracks, and then the next day there was simultaneous moving out of the JNA command at Bistrik, and this transport of Izetbegovic to the Presidency. As far as I can recollect, this event and the one we are now discussing did not occur on the same day, so that this column which was coming out, headed by General Kukajac, from the command and the other one from Lukavica. That is one event. And the other one is when trams were set alight, and when on the 2nd of May in the city of Sarajevo, the war began.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And when was that other event that you said -- that you mentioned when there were soldiers in the column as well as Mr. Alija Izetbegovic? Was that on the 3rd of May?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: On the 2nd of May, you said that citizens were killed, that they were shooting from the Presidency building towards the banks and the Marsal Tito barracks.

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say towards the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, the tanks then. Were soldiers in the column killed on that occasion, as you were an eyewitness?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't an eyewitness of the actual battle, of the actual fighting. I was at Marijin Dvor, and this was happening at Skenderija. This is several hundred metres away. But it was shown on television that evening, some soldiers were killed. And several APCs and tanks were destroyed and set on fire. But on the other side, on the buildings, there were traces of shells that were fired from those tanks, most probably, but I wasn't the -- a direct eyewitness of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: What do you know about the event when president Alija Izetbegovic was in the column? Were there any incidents on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was covered by television. And according to my recollection, an incident occurred when the column from the command at the Bistrik and the other one with president Izetbegovic in it, under the control of the UN - everything was happening under their control - when an incident occurred and conflict began. But I don't recollect the details, because I only saw it on television. The situation was already stressful. And there was a lot of fear that I felt and all the other citizens as to what was going on, and that was in fact when the war began in earnest. It was inconceivable somehow that the JNA should exchange its own general for the president of the Presidency who had actually been captured the night before in the barracks, who had been held there together with Zlatko Lagomdzija, who in those days was in opposition to the ruling national parties.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge that on that occasion, president Alija Izetbegovic arrived from Lisbon, that nobody came to great him at the airport, and that the army, in order to protect him, kept him at the Lukavica barracks?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You would have to ask him as well as the military who held him because interpretations of that event differed in the media, and I really do not have any direct knowledge of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that throughout the time of conflict in Sarajevo, the media carried various misinformation and different interpretations of various events?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course there was misinformation, and there was even such a report that the son of Karadzic had joined the BH army, and we believed it for two days, and then we realised it was wartime propaganda by the Bosnian media. And as to what was being reported about Sarajevo in the media by Pale, Belgrade, and other stations, as we were living there, we knew how much there was that was -- that were falsehoods and false interpretations. It is well known that in wartime, the truth is the first casualty. What one lives through and sees with one's own eyes and one hears with one's own ears is one's own conception of the truth, and that is all I can talk about. What the media reported is up to the media.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that you told us that you took part in the work of the War Presidency, did you know that at the level of the republic, the Territorial Defence issued an order to attack all barracks and capture or appropriate the military property -- the military assets from those barracks?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the level of the republic, it was the Presidency of the Bosnia and Herzegovina who made the decisions, and I hear of such a decision for the first time from you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that you watched and followed the media. Did you know from the media or from personal knowledge that there was a mortar attack on the Marsal Tito barracks and that all the barracks in town were attacked on the 2nd of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know from personal knowledge is that there were no such attacks. What the media reported, I don't know. But that in an atmosphere of tension that started following the referendum, it is possible that such conflicts occurred. I'm not denying it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in the JNA barracks, in those days - and when I say "those days," I mean the period from the 19th of May, 1992, when the JNA army left Sarajevo - was the water supply and the electricity supply cut off to the barracks?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as I know, no, it was not. The Presidency of the city came into being later. But unlike the media interpretations from Croatia, this did not occur in Bosnia-Herzegovina because the JNA until these events was considered to be our army.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Until when was it considered to be your army?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until after the 2nd of May, 1992, in my opinion. It was an army which would preserve peace, even if it were to remain only a Serb army, that is, an army in which all the officers and soldiers are Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that the army, the JNA, had already in March taken up positions on Mojmilo hill where the water reservoir was. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I said. And as far as I remember, that was prior to these events on the 2nd of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge as to which brigade that was?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which brigade it was, but it was reported in the media that it was a unit from Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, when I interrupted the witness, I apologise, but I would like to make a break rather soon. So if you would finish with this question or perhaps the next question, see whether there's a proper moment to stop. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know that the brigade that was at Mojmilo at the time was under the command of Hadzihasanovic, who was the commander of that brigade?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned that later from the media. But at the time, he was a JNA officer, and as such, he was given orders, and he acted accordingly, at least, that was how it was reported, that he captured those high features above the new part of the city, including the water reservoir at Mojmilo.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you agree with me that the water reservoir was protected at the time by the JNA so that the citizens of Sarajevo should have water?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reservoirs should be protected by the water supply staff. There was no need for the JNA to protect it. And this caused fear among the people, local people. Why should the army and guns and cannons protect the water reservoir? If such protection was necessary, it should have been done by the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know what was situated on the other side of the Mojmilo hill? Because one part of Mojmilo hill faces Dobrinja. What about the other side of Mojmilo hill?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the other side of the hill Ali Pasino Polje, another settlement and Ali Pasino bridge? And further on towards Trebevic is the Lukavica barracks, which is some 30 kilometres from that hill.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, is this a good place to stop? Thank you very much. Before the break, I would just like to remind you that of course we lost a couple of minutes with these translation problems. As far as I understand, on the 29th of November, the co-counsel has been informed about the procedures. And since I am quite sure he wants to avoid as much loss of time as I want to avoid it, I would urge both parties always to give any original text prior to the beginning of the Court session so that the interpreters' booth has available this text already. Then I would like to have a break for -- I would say until quarter to 6.00, if that's fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So everyone is present, apart from the witness. I would just like to make one remark at this moment. As I indicated, after Mr. Kupusovic has been examined by the parties, I would like to have a short Status Conference, because some issues still have to be discussed. In order to -- not to lose too much time, I would finish today by just five minutes closed session in order to see whether all the parties have got everything they need for this Status Conference, that all the documents are there, that we know what we are talking about, in order not to lose any time if it comes tomorrow to this Status Conference. So the last five minutes will be reserved for that and will be in closed session. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Mr. Usher, will you please bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, whilst the witness is being brought in, might I clarify that comment that you have just made. Are you proposing to have a Status Conference tonight or tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to have a Pre-Status Conference today in order to make quite sure that no one comes up tomorrow saying, well, I haven't got this document. I don't know whether there is still a motion pending on that. Just so that we know exactly what we are talking about tomorrow. We are not going to discuss any motions today. Perhaps we may make a few remarks. But so that everyone is well prepared, in order to avoid any loss of time tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The Defence would like, prior to the continuation of the cross-examination, to tender Document -- "The Battle for Sarajevo," page 76, which we read out, and the witness confirmed the names that were familiar to him. He knows Ramiz. He spoke about the tanks. And the Defence would like to tender this page of the book, page 76, into evidence as Exhibit D/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution would offer an objection in respect of that on the basis, again, of an evidential foundation. It is the fact that whilst certain names were simply known to the witness, and he said he had seen some columns of tanks, nothing in what he said in response to my learned friend indicated any link between his knowledge and the actual contents of this text and article as such. And as a result, the Prosecution would object on the basis of a failure to establish evidential foundation to introduce this as an exhibit in the trial to be taken into account by Your Honours as a matter of evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As you may have noticed, Mr. Blaxill, my attention was drawn for one moment by the court manager. So if you would allow me just to read the transcript on question, the remark you just made. If you can give me half a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: After I have consulted my colleagues, we invite the Defence to explain to this Chamber what the relevance is of this document in view of the answers given to the questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness confirmed that he knows Mr. Kerim Loncarevic, that he was a deputy together with him, that he knows that he was the commander of a unit, checking the credibility of the witness, the witness would like, in this way -- sorry, the Defence would like to call in question the testimony of this witness who yesterday and today described all the details and appeared to have knowledge about everything that went on in Sarajevo. It is the position of the Defence that the witness, in view of his role in the War Presidency, knew what was going on in Sarajevo and how certain paramilitary units behaved in Sarajevo. The Defence considers this document to be relevant as evidence for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we may interject with just one, one or two points here. To the best of my recollection s regards to the evidence given by Mr. Kupusovic, he certainly has conceded to my learned friend that he knew the gentleman Loncarevic, the apparent author of this text. I do not recall him stating that he knew, and I do stand to be corrected if I am wrong, but I don't recall him saying that he knew that the man led a unit of any kind of military or paramilitary. And indeed, I do recall that Mr. Kupusovic indicated that the Presidency to which he belonged was a city Presidency and was a purely civilian affair and that it was the state level War Presidency that dealt with all matters military, and he did state that in his evidence in chief. I therefore would contest the idea that he by virtue of what has now been said can be deemed to be someone who had knowledge of all military matters that went on in Sarajevo. He spoke exclusively as the experience of civilians and civilian authorities. That's my recollection, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand what you mean. As far as I do understand the Defence is that using this text, they are aiming at demonstrating that the witness was far more detailed in his statements on the questions that were put to him yesterday, and that he is less in detail on what he -- on the questions that have been put to him today. So without going into any detail on every single line of the -- of what Ms. Pilipovic has said about relevance is true or not, I stay out of that. But on the basis of that intention, the Chamber will accept this document as an exhibit, which of course doesn't say anything about any probative value either of the document or of any statement later on. So the objection is rejected, and please, Ms. Pilipovic, would you proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that you were a member of the War Presidency. Will you tell us what your duties were in that War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a member of the Presidency of the city assembly in wartime, and that is why I accepted the term you used, "War Presidency," though with regard to any military matters, it was not a War Presidency. In addition to the town mayor and the deputy mayor, who was a lady and who chaired the Presidency meetings, the other members did not have any specific responsibilities except for the fact that in view of my expertise, I was more involved in dealing with matters of water supply for the city.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: What was the situation with respect to water supply in March, April, and May? Was the water turned off, and was there a shortage of water?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the water supply was regular.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that in April and May, there were incidents and clashes which escalated, according to what you said, on the 2nd of May, 1992. In those days, were there any movements of the population in the sense that Serbs from parts of the town where the Muslims were in the majority moved to parts of the town where the Serbs were in a majority, and the Muslims to the urban part of the city where the Muslims were in the majority?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no such population movements within the city. But already in March and April, there were Muslim refugees coming from villages around Sarajevo who thought they would be safer in town. And that they were not safe in those villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge of the Serbs leaving the urban part of the city, as you call it, and leaving Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said, and I repeat, that a couple of thousand of citizens of Sarajevo, before the 2nd of May, when the railroad and air traffic was discontinued, left the city, but this applied to all citizens regardless of ethnic origin. But there were probably more Serbs percentage-wise than in the town as a whole because the families of Serb officers were leaving. Those were the reports in the media, though I'm sure no one has precise data about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that a separation line was established between the Serb and Muslim part of the city, or Bosniak part of the city?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no such thing as a Serb and a Muslim part of the city, and no such lines were established.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that a separation line was established in relation to the Grbavica district which had a majority Serb population?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Grbavica did not have a majority Serb population, but there were quite a number of JNA officers living at Grbavica, and the line with Grbavica was established after the barracks was evacuated as the part of the town under the control of the army of Republika Srpska, which accounts for about 25 -- 5 percent of the area of the city.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did the Croats of Sarajevo organise themselves as the HVO?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a party, the HDZ was established in Sarajevo, and as far as I can remember, the HVO appeared sometime in May or June 1992, as did the HOS, H-O-S, as an organisation whose members were predominantly Croat.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In what part of the towns were the Croats mostly concentrated?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nowhere in particular except, as I have mentioned, in the village of Stup, which after the second world war, became a component part of the city so that locally, there were several thousands Croats living there, and on a local level, they were in the majority. But as soon as you went beyond that, the population was mixed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In Sarajevo was there a conflict between the Croats and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: According to your knowledge, would you agree with me when I say that Sarajevo was divided up into a city with a majority Serb population, the Muslim part of town and the Croatian part of town? Would you agree with me there?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at all. Just Grbavica after the control was taken over from the army of Republika Srpska. After the army of Republika Srpska took control, it became a majority Serb area because the others left. The Muslims and Croats who had lived there left their apartments without anything, and they had to leave that part of town, move to another part of town, or to move through the territory under the control of the army Republika Srpska on to third countries.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: What about the Ilidza Vogosca Trnovo municipalities?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were municipalities which were located in -- around the urban part of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Under whose control were those particular municipalities? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The municipality of Trnovo, as far as I remember, a couple of times changed from being under the control of the army of Republika Srpska and the BH army and vice versa. Whereas Ilidza and Vogosca, throughout that time, as settlements, were under the control of the army of Republika Srpska. But parts of the territory of those municipalities were also controlled by the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: What about the Pale municipality?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pale municipality was throughout under the control of the army of Republika Srpska. Most of the municipality, a part of it towards the Drina river, was under the control of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: What about the Stari Grad, Novo Sarajevo, and Centar? Those municipalities, what about them?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation there was similar but opposite. The urban part of town where the population lived, they were under an encirclement. Whereas parts of the municipalities which stretched towards the mountains and were sparsely populated, and the sparsely populated areas around the city itself, were under the control of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned mountains. Which mountains were they? Which of the mountains surrounding Sarajevo, in fact?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Trebevic, Ozren, Jahorina, Romanija. Then on the other side, Bukovik, Treposko and the peaks of Bukovik stretching towards -- and of course Mount Igman.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and of course Mount Igman. What are the dominant hills around Sarajevo? You said Mojmilo hill. Would you agree with me, that that is -- there was Debelo Brdo, Colina Kapa, Zuc, and Hum, that those were the hills?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, those were the dominant hills, but I would add Spicasta Stijena.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: During the conflict in Sarajevo, under whose control were those hills?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These hills were under the control of the JNA, and later on the army of Republika Srpska. But Zuc hill, in the fighting between the BH army units and the Republika Srpska army was won by these units in the defence of the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: What about Hum hill?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hum hill throughout that time -- actually it is almost in town, and that is where the television antenna is and tower, and it was targeted in April by JNA planes and rockets. But as a hill within the city, it remained throughout in the encirclement that was positioned around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Which army was on and around the hill?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the top of the hill was the television tower. There was no army there. And later on, there were UN units stationed there. And around the hill, or rather, in the settlements around the hill, when it was established, it was under the control of the units of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: What about Colina Kapa, big and small, Velika Colina Kapa? Under whose control was that? And what area of Sarajevo can be seen from those hills?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Velika and Mala Colina Kapa, parts of Trebevic. I don't know the details. But they were somewhere around the demarcation line. I think that Velika Colina Kapa was always under the control of the army of Republika Srpska, whereas the Mala Colina Kapa, which is a little lower, was practically no man's land in between, because underneath Mala Colina Kapa were the first houses, and that was where the defence of Sarajevo was. And after that, we have forest land, and the slopes of Trebevic, which is where the snipers and artillery of the Republika Srpska army were located.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned snipers belonging to the army of Republika Srpska. Do you happen to know that the Muslim paramilitary formations at the beginning and later on the BH army had snipers?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to the beginning, I don't know about that. I know nothing about that. But later on, as the army developed during the war, in the media, news of that kind was broadcast, but I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: While you were performing your functions in the War Presidency, you had contacts with the Territorial Defence of the city. You were -- you dealt with the organisation of the water supply system and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I hate to interrupt, but I object to -- in this sense of using War Presidency. I think it's leading to confusion with the state War Presidency. The witness has given a distinction between the two, and I think he denied knowledge of military matters as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you be able to, Ms. Pilipovic, to rephrase your question in such a way that any confusion will be avoided?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness agreed with the Defence that after the proclamation of the general mobilisation at the level of the town, a War Presidency was functioning. The witness and the Defence agreed upon that. I'm not asking him about military matters; I'm just asking him about the functioning of the Territorial Defence of the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you are talking about a War Presidency, you mean to say the Presidency that was functioning at the time of war? Is that what you mean to say? Is that acceptable to the Prosecution in order to avoid any misunderstanding? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my learned colleague has just brought my attention to the fact that the names of the mountains have not been recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps I explain that to you. Sometimes names, it takes a bit more time, and during this evening or overnight, these names - even of mountains - rocks are very solid, as you know. They will be there in proper order tomorrow in the transcript, and you can check it then. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge as to the fact that on the territory of the city of Sarajevo, a factory called Zrak existed?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In which part of Sarajevo was that?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's under Mojmilo hill.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: During the conflict in Sarajevo, who controlled that part of town, that part of Sarajevo where the Zrak factory was located?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is in the town itself and was inaccessible throughout that time, directly to those who had encircled the town, which is to say that it was located in town.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the factory produced weapons?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that before the war, it produced optical instruments for the Yugoslav people's army.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: What about during the war, in that part of town, did it produce optical sights, optic sights?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. But I don't think it was working during the war because it had nothing to work with.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know the name of Stjepan Siber? Does that ring a bell, and did you happen to encounter him during the conflicts in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know the name Stjepan Siber, and I did have occasion to meet him several times in the joint commission which went to the airport for negotiations with the opposite side.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I am going to show you a book written by Mr. Stjepan Siber. It is called "Deceptions, misconceptions and the Truth," and it is a wartime diary kept by Mr. Stjepan Siber, published in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just to ensure that the interpreters' booth has a copy, and we will be provided with a copy as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The previous document will be Exhibit D1, and the English translation will be D1.1.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission, I should like to read two lines from that book, from that wartime diary. It is the 16th of May, 1992, the entry for the 16th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you please wait until they have got the copies so they can better follow your reading. Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: "The 16th of May, at a high level meeting of commanders, we conclude that 540 pieces of sniper rifles from the Zrak factory were equally distributed to the units in the defence of the city." Witness, may I ask you my question pursuant to that?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: My question is: Do you know that 550 sniper rifles from the Zrak factory was distributed to units in the city?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You have told us that -- can you tell us how many barracks there were in the former JNA in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a number of barracks, 10, 15, if you count some of the smaller facilities of the JNA, warehouses or things like that. 15 to 20 in town, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know where they were located and how many soldiers there were in the barracks?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea as to the number of soldiers, but the largest barracks was the Marsal Tito barracks, and then there was the command of the city at Bistrik, the JNA command, and there was a barracks at Vratnik, and one in Nedzarici, and some other barracks which I don't exactly know Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. where they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what was in Rajlovac?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a sports airfield in Rajlovac, and also a military part, section of the airport before the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that during the conflict, those barracks were used by the soldiers of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which barracks you mean, you have in mind. The Marsal Tito barracks, the JNA left the Marsal Tito barracks and then the special police and de-mining unit was set up there and was used partially by the BH army and the United Nations forces. It was -- the rest was under the control of -- Rajlovac was under the control of the army of Republika Srpska. And when the JNA moved out of the barracks, like in the Marsal Tito barracks, it shelled it from the positions around town. And they remained as ruins, or as seriously destroyed facilities. And they were used in town -- in that state for the requirements of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us where the Supreme Command of the BH army was located?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that at a time it was in the Vranica company in that building. Otherwise I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: The Vranica company was a civilian facility, a civilian building, was it not?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that the Supreme Command of the BH army was set up in a civilian facility?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the building of the administration of a large civil engineering firm. As far as I know, the command of the army moved in in the autumn in 1992 because the building was quite empty. The company was no longer working and there was nobody there in the building. So it became a military facility from that time on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, where the staff and headquarters of the 1st Corps of the BH army was located?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The staff and headquarters of the 1st Corps, well that was established only later on. For a time it was in the headquarters of the territorial Defence at Ciglane, that part of town where the territorial Defence was located before the war. And somewhere towards the end of the war, it was moved to the Zrak company.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to know that the members of the Muslim paramilitary forces and later on the members of the BH army used civilian buildings and facilities for their own purposes?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of any Muslim paramilitary forces. And likewise, I know nothing about the use of civilian facilities for military purposes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to know what parts of town and what facilities were the staffs of the brigades set up, the core of the army? And there were more than ten of them, let me remind you.

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a number of those staffs in the course of the war, and they moved around. But as the civilian Presidency of the city, we had no part in that, and I personally have no knowledge of where the commands of the individual brigades and the 1st Corps in particular were set up and where they moved around during the war, which facilities they occupied.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many soldiers the BH army corps consisted of?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that towards the end of the war the figure bandied about was 40.000 soldiers with the proviso that two-thirds of that was said to be outside the encirclement, and about 10 or 15.000 were in town. But those were facts and figures published by the media. I have no personal knowledge of that subject.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You said that there was -- police were in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the police force was put up in the police facilities and buildings, which means in the police stations that existed before the war and also in some other houses next to the first lines of defence, the first front lines. I know that because regardless of the fact that the Presidency of the town had no competencies over the police, we did cooperate for purposes of law and order in the city itself in battling with crime and the black market. So the police there assisted our own inspections in that respect frequently.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to know what the soldiers of the BH army wore? How were they clothed? That is to say, the soldiers in Sarajevo, did they all wear military uniforms?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning, no, they did not. They didn't have any uniforms, and then these uniforms were established with the insignia of the BH army. And regardless of the shortage of uniforms, the soldiers did have the insignia of the lily, the crest with the lily. Later on they had different uniforms which were of different cuts and colours, but all with the emblems and insignia of the lily with crossed swords, the crossed sword and lily emblem of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the lily being the insignia of Bosnia-Herzegovina and crossed swords of the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So that means all of them had military uniforms?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that not at the beginning. There were no uniforms at the beginning, just the insignia, but as the war developed, soldiers could be recognised by the uniforms they wore. But they would very rarely move around town. They were units who were on the fringes of the city providing a defence for the town. And it was only in the second half of the war or thereabouts that we can say that all of them had uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Were you personally a military recruit, or did you have any military assignment, conscript?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I was -- I did not do my military service in the JNA for health reasons; I was not a military conscript. I was unfit for service. And when the Presidency of the city was established at the beginning of June 1992, that was my work assignment at the same time. And I had my assignments -- work assignments at the university and at the institute as director until I became the mayor in March 1994, when that became my professional duty and preoccupation.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In March 1994, you said you had a work assignment, and that in 1994, you became mayor. In 1992 and 1993, in view of the fact that we agreed that an army did exist, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the army of Republika Srpska with the Romanija Corps, until you had become mayor, in that period before you became mayor, was there fighting in town between those, if I can call them that, two armies?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was fighting around the city, and a number of attempts to lift the siege and encirclement. And in the town itself, at Grbavica, the demarcation line there at Grbavica, there was constant fighting the between two armies. There was fighting between the two armies.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that at the Ciglane, the tunnel leading out of the town, that a tank had been deployed there?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In that period of time, that is to say before you, yourself, became mayor, was there any substantial movement in the demarcation line?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing that happened was that the hill of Zuc was liberated. As to other movements, they were very slight, either to the detriment of the town or towards expanding the territory within the city.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: During that time, did you go to Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the summer of 1993, I went for the first time after May the 1st, 1992. I managed to go to Dobrinja to find photographs and other mementos from my burnt apartment in Dobrinja, and you had to go there through trenches because that was the line of defence of the city. And I went there as a civilian, as an ordinary citizen, to collect some toys for the children and some other mementoes, from what remained of my apartment, the one I used to live in.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You said that it was Dobrinja I. Under control whose was Dobrinja I at the time that you went in 1993?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was under control of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And what about the Dobrinja II, III, IV, and V?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Almost the whole of Dobrinja was under the control of the BH army except for the part right next to Lukavica, the barracks in Lukavica. So that a part of Dobrinja I was under the control of the BH army, and the other part behind the side street leading to the main street was under the control of the Republika Srpska so that the building I lived in was actually on the front line of defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: While you were town mayor of Sarajevo, did the city receive humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Who did that humanitarian aid come from?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Humanitarian aid to the city of Sarajevo itself, independently from the UNHRC and other international humanitarian organisations, was sent by cities all over the world which sympathised with the suffering of the people of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did Serbs receive that humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean those living in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course they did. Humanitarian aid was distributed in Sarajevo regardless of ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that in the urban part of Sarajevo, about 30 to 40.000 Serbs had remained. Could those Serbs leave Sarajevo and could they go to Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the end of the war, the assessment was that some 40.000 Serbs remained, but during the first two years of the war that we are discussing, there were more Serbs. Out of the 120.000 before the war living in Sarajevo, in the part that was under siege gradually and precisely because of the calls by SDS leader, and the possibility during cease-fires to cross to Grbavica or other parts outside the encirclement Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. around Sarajevo, whoever wanted could leave the city. And after that first winter, and also after the second winter, quite a number of citizens of all ethnicities left the city. But no one prevented the Serbs or others from leaving whenever that was possible, when there was no fighting around town and when those surrounding the city allowed the evacuation of children and other citizens from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Was special permission required for leaving town?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In some periods, yes, permission was required from the military authorities because of the military obligation that existed. But I personally, and the city Presidency was against it. But was not directly involved in any way with that. We frequently requested that people be allowed to leave the city, people who could help in raising humanitarian aid for Sarajevo and the reconstruction of the infrastructure. And we asked the military authorities to do this, and they were the ones who sometimes gave us as members of the city Presidency permission and sometimes they didn't. Sometimes this was enforced; sometimes it was not. There was no constant prohibition on leaving town, but the situation changed during the war, depending on the situation on the war front, and the position taken by the authorities of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Who gave permission for people to leave the city?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were known as the municipal staffs, or the municipal commands, of the Secretariat for Defence in the municipalities of the city that were part of the republic Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any knowledge that certain Serbs, who held senior positions, who were doctors in hospitals, were arrested when they tried to leave Sarajevo or were held in prisoners?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us today that there were periods when there was truce in town. Could you tell us a little more about that, at what level was such agreement reached, how long they lasted, and who violated them?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The cease-fires were negotiated at a higher level than the city Presidency, therefore at the level of the army command or the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And according to my knowledge, those cease-fires were always violated on the part of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You said, according to your knowledge, where does that knowledge come from?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were in the city, and when somebody attacked the city, that meant that somebody from the outside had broken the cease-fire. And that means the army of Republika Srpska. I have no knowledge that ever during a cease-fire was an attempt made to make a breakthrough through the encirclement as a violation of the cease-fire. It was in our interest to have a cease-fire because of water supplies, electricity, repairs in town, and the position of the civilians in the town as opposed to the continuation of the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In Sarajevo, were Serbs also exposed to shelling and sniping as were the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And did you have occasion to see the weaponry of the BH army, where they were positioned in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no weapons depots in Sarajevo throughout the duration of the war. But I would occasionally see rifles or mortars carried by soldiers of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge as to where those weapons were kept?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And where would you see them?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For instance, when an attempt to break into the city was made from Trebevic, then units from the other side of the city came to the assistance of the defenders in that part of the city, and then you would see soldiers running along the streets carrying rifles and mortars and some other weapons, which I don't know what they were exactly. But in any event, they were weapons that soldiers could carry.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Where were those soldiers that you saw accommodated?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The soldiers of the BH army did not have any barracks in the city of Sarajevo except partially those evacuated by the JNA, so they were put up in trenches and houses along those trenches on the outskirts of the city where the defence lines were. That is where they would be in shifts of five to ten days, and then they would go home to their own homes to spend a few days with their families.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that those houses and facilities used by soldiers of the BH army, those civilian houses, were, in fact, military objects?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were civilian houses when they were lived in by people who had to flee from there because of the attacks from the outside. Therefore, from the encirclement, so that those abandoned or half destroyed houses with basements were military targets when the soldiers were in them. But there were no civilians in them any more.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us today that at the level of the city, there was a public health institute?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we used to call it the Institute for Hygiene.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Quite. When was it established?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, A long time ago. Maybe 50 years ago. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Was it functioning throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that on the basis of data obtained from that Institute for Hygiene, you mentioned the number of casualties in the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Who provided data to that Institute of Hygiene?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Institute of Hygiene collected those data, according to its own methodology, from people in the field, and on the basis of reports received from hospitals, funeral parlours, and other institutions that had any such information. And then to avoid duplication of names, the institute would review them and officially submit reports to the Presidency of the city and very often these were published in the newspapers. The director of that institute will be able to tell you more about the methodology as the institute -- he was the director of that institute throughout the war and his name is Meztic [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that 90 percent of the casualties were civilians, if I remember correctly, please correct me, and 10 percent were soldiers.

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I said 95 percent or roughly, according to my own estimate, because we don't have the figures for the military as to how many people were killed as soldiers, because what I was just saying about those lines, those men, those soldiers who would be soldiers for ten days and for five days at home in their houses then they would be civilians because they were not armed, they were on leave after those efforts. So if they were killed while they were at home or going to fetch water for their families or to fetch bread, they were killed as civilians. If those same people were killed on the defence lines wearing uniforms and carrying weapons, then they were soldiers. So that our overall estimate of us as the presidency and later was that roughly only 5 percent of the citizens of Sarajevo were killed as soldiers and 95 percent as civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You just told me that in town there were 25.000 soldiers?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said 10 to 15.000.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I apologise. Where were those soldiers who participated in the fighting and who were wounded? Where were they treated?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were treated in one of these two hospitals or in military clinics which were right next to the defence lines. Or if this happened on Mount Igman, they were driven to Konjic, the hospital there, because they couldn't be transported to the city itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So from Sarajevo, the wounded would leave Sarajevo and be taken to Konjic?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, from the other side of the encirclement, from Mount Igman, they couldn't pass through the tunnel, through the below the airport runway so they couldn't go through the encirclement around town and into town, but were taken much further away to Konjic. As for those who were wounded within the encirclement, they were treated in the hospitals within the city.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: How did you gain possession of that information, as you were not involved in military affairs? Did you discuss these matters at the level of the presidency?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The hospitals, of course, and the doctors and the medical staff were also within the terms of reference of the city Presidency. I didn't concern myself only with water, but with all other matters as well. And as for the treatment, it was common knowledge to all the citizens of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that there was no electricity, water, or gas in the city. Could you explain to me whether a cut in the electricity causes suspension of the water supply?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us there were 11 transformer stations in the territory under the control of the army of Republika Srpska. Can you explain if the transformer stations were in the area controlled by Republika Srpska, how could the electricity supply be cut and the water supply? Or were those transformer stations damaged, and then mixed commissions went to establish who and how would make the repairs?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes the transformer stations were damaged, more frequently the long-distance transmission lines which supply the transformer stations with power. But most of the electricity cuts were not provoked by those Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. damages. But as far as I know from this commission and in the city, electricity was cut intentionally for units of the army that were in town, those ten or so thousand men to be left without electricity, but the city as such was left without any power supply, and thereby, also without water because water had to be pumped from the main source to the town, and this was switched on or switched off at their will by the people who controlled that; that is, civilians under the control of the army of Republika Srpska manning those objects or by the military themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, would you please try to finish this part of your cross-examination either at this moment or within, let's say, one or two or three minutes so that we can discuss other matters for just the time that is still available, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will, in a couple of minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: If there is no electricity, and if it is switched off in the urban part of Sarajevo where the BH corps was accommodated, could there be electricity in the part of Sarajevo that was under the control of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The settlement in the broader area of Sarajevo had electricity much more frequently. And in Grbavica, electricity would be cut also because there was no supply in the centre of town. However, later, Republika Srpska made lines to provide Grbavica with electricity while the town itself was without electricity.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: What about the water reservoir at Mojmilo? It was under the control of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime in the autumn of 1992, through conflicts, the BH army gained control of it. And until then, it was under the control of the JNA or the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Was the water supply cut in that part?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. In those days, I don't know, because there was water until the autumn of 1992 in old town with some interruptions. But nothing like what it was later when the city was left totally without water for longer periods of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And what about gas? Was there gas while the conflict was ongoing?

utterances.speaker: TARIK KUPUSOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first winter of war 1992/1993, there was gas. And later, it was available but with interruptions and with the pressure being lower.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Pilipovic. Perhaps this is the moment where we -- you could tender in evidence the second document. Although we said it would be at the end of the cross-examination, perhaps we do it better now at the end of this day, although cross-examination has not yet finished. Have you got any idea how much time you still need, Ms. Pilipovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another half hour, Your Honour, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Pilipovic. You tender the document you gave to the witness this afternoon in evidence? Is there any number related to it yet? No number. The Prosecution, any objections, apart from those?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Are we referring to the second document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the second document because the first document has been dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes, I would reiterate the Prosecution objection there. It is simply a matter that there has been no concrete evidence adduced to indicate the production of these weapons and the distribution of them to the army, and it's something to which the witness could not agree. He had absolutely no knowledge of it. Again, he doesn't appear to be in any way a suitable vehicle for simply a piece of paper to be adduced which has no evidential value on the face of it as being just an extract. It's not even in a greater context; it's just a little extract from a piece of personal writing. As a result, we would consider it so unreliable as to be unacceptable and inadmissible, bearing in mind already Your Honour's comment earlier as regards taking your own judicial view of probative value. I would suggest that a document of this type in this way has none whatsoever. And it would be improper to adduce through this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, would you please respond to this objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is the position of the Defence that this is a relevant document for the Defence and the Chamber, especially in view of the fact that during the testimony of this witness, the witness is familiar with military matters. He knows that there were snipers, and he has knowledge about these things, so that we cannot accept the objection of the Prosecution, that it is sufficient for the witness simply to say "I don't know." This is, after all, a document, a book, by Mr. Stjepan Siber that the witness is familiar with, he knows. He lived in Sarajevo. He took part in the negotiations. And he was able to make decisions at this level. The witness knows this. And the witness confirmed that the Zrak factory was in the territory under the control of the BH army in that part of Sarajevo that was controlled by the BH army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber would like to have more time to consider the question, so we'll give a decision on that by tomorrow, whether it will be admitted in evidence or not. So it is not yet admitted at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I have another -- first of all, the witness is excused for this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For very practical reasons, I suggest to the parties that we'll have not a formal five-minute Status Conference, but we will have a five-minute closed session, because for a Status Conference, all the videotapes have to be changed, et cetera. So that will be -- I suggest that we have a closed session for five minutes and discuss exactly what we would have discussed in the Status Conference, as I suggested before. So could we please -- I see the court manager is already taking all the necessary measures. Thank you.
